en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the All-Knowing Wisdom within the Section of Puzzling Questions.
6. The Question on the Benefits of the Development of Loving-kindness “Venerable Nāgasena, this has been said by the Blessed One:

‘Monks, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness is pursued, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, eleven benefits are to be expected.’”
Which eleven? One sleeps happily; one awakens happily; one does not see evil dreams; one is dear to human beings;

one is dear to non-human beings; deities protect one; fire, poison, or weapons do not affect one; [one’s mind remains clear]; [one dies unconfused]; [and if one does not penetrate further, one is reborn in a happy destination].
‘The mind quickly becomes concentrated, the complexion brightens, one dies unconfused,
and if one does not penetrate further, one goes to the Brahma-world.
Yet again, you say:
‘Prince Sāma, dwelling in loving-kindness, while wandering in the forest surrounded by a herd of deer, was struck by King Pīḷiyakkha with a poisoned arrow; he fainted right there and fell.
If, venerable Nāgasena, it was said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, through loving-kindness... [and so forth].
"…he goes to the Brahma-world. In that case, the statement that "Prince Sāma, while dwelling in loving-kindness and wandering in the forest surrounded by a herd of deer,
was pierced by King Pīḷiyakkha with a poison-smeared arrow and fell down right there in a swoon," is false.

If Prince Sāma, while dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettā*) and wandering in the forest surrounded by a herd of deer, was pierced by King Pīḷiyakkha with a poison-saturated arrow and fell down right there in a swoon, then that statement—“By loving-kindness, monks...
[the blade does not cut]”—is false.
This too is a double-edged question, most subtle, refined, delicate, and profound, even for those humans who are highly skilled.

“May he release his limbs from the sweat; he has arrived before you. Untangle that which is entangled in the great tangle! Grant the eye to the sons of the Conqueror who have not yet come, for their attainment of Nibbāna.
“This too, Great King, was spoken by the Blessed One:”
“Monks, through loving-kindness...
[as before] ...or even the sword does not strike.

Prince Sāma, dwelling in loving-kindness, was wandering in the forest surrounded by a herd of deer when he was struck by King Pīliyakkha with a poisoned arrow; he fell down right there in a swoon. But in this matter, Great King, there is a reason.
What is the reason for this?

Great King, these qualities do not belong to the person; rather, these qualities belong to the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*). Great King, at the moment Prince Sāma was lifting the water-jar, he was distracted from the cultivation of loving-kindness.
Great King, at whatever moment a person has entered into a state of loving-kindness, fire, poison, or a weapon does not affect that person at that moment.
Whatever persons might wish him harm, upon approaching, do not see him; they find no opportunity against him.
These qualities, Great King, do not belong to the person; these qualities belong to the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Here, Great King, suppose a man who is a hero in battle were to enter the fray after donning an impenetrable suit of armor.
When arrows are shot at him, they fall scattered upon reaching him; they find no opening in him.
Great King, this is not the merit of the hero in battle, but rather the merit of his impenetrable armor and mail, that arrows, when shot, fall scattered upon reaching him.
In the same way, Great King, these are not the merits of the person; these are the merits of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Great King, at whatever moment a person has entered into a state of loving-kindness (*mettā*), fire, poison, or weapons do not affect that person at that moment.

Whatever beings desire his harm, upon approaching him, do not see him; they find no opening against him. Great King, these are not the virtues of the person; rather, these are the virtues of the cultivation of loving-kindness."
"Furthermore, Great King, suppose a man were to hold in his hand the root of a divine invisibility potion. As long as that root remains in his hand, no ordinary person would see him.
This, Great King, is not a quality of the man; it is a quality of the invisibility potion that he does not appear within the range of vision of ordinary people.
In the same way, Great King, these are not qualities of the individual; these are qualities of the cultivation of loving-kindness."
"At whatever moment, Great King, a person has entered upon a state of loving-kindness, at that moment neither fire, nor poison, nor weapon affects that person.
Whatever beings desire his harm, even if they approach him, do not see him; they find no opportunity against him.
These qualities, Great King, do not belong to the person; these qualities belong to the cultivation of loving-kindness."
Or again, great king, just as when a man has entered a well-constructed large shelter,
a massive rain-cloud pouring down cannot wet him— this, great king, is not the merit of the man, but the merit of the large shelter, in that the massive rain-cloud,
though pouring down, does not wet him.
“In the same way, Great King, these qualities do not belong to the person; rather, these qualities belong to the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
At whatever moment, Great King, a person has entered into a state of loving-kindness, at that moment neither fire, nor poison, nor weapon can affect that person.

Should anyone wishing him harm approach him, they do not even see him, and they are unable to inflict any harm upon him. These, Great King, are not qualities of the person; these qualities belong to the cultivation of loving-kindness.”
“It is wonderful, venerable Nāgasena! It is marvelous, venerable Nāgasena! The cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) is a warding off of all evil.

“The cultivation of loving-kindness, great king, brings about all wholesome qualities; it is beneficial both to those who are dear and to those who are not. For all those beings who are bound by consciousness, the cultivation of loving-kindness is of great advantage and should be shared with all.
This is the sixth question, concerning the benefits of the cultivation of loving-kindness.
